questions.stem: A transformer can be used to change

options.text: both a.c. and d.c. voltages equally well
direct current into a magnetic field without induction

questions.explanation: A transformer relies on a changing flux in the core to induce an e.m.f. in the secondary. Only an alternating primary current produces a continuously changing flux. Steady d.c. gives a constant flux, so ΔΦ/Δt = 0 and the secondary voltage is zero (apart from a brief pulse at the instant of switching).

distractorRationale.b: D.c. does not produce a continuously changing flux, so a transformer cannot step d.c. voltages
distractorRationale.c: The two are not equal: a.c. works, steady d.c. does not
distractorRationale.d: A current does produce a magnetic field, but that is not what a transformer is for, and without a changing field there is no induced secondary voltage

questions.stem: Eddy currents in a transformer core are reduced by

options.text: winding the coils with thin high-resistance wire

questions.explanation: The changing flux induces e.m.f.s not only in the secondary but also in the core itself. Those circulating eddy currents heat the core. Slicing the core into thin sheets, insulated from one another (laminations), breaks up the eddy paths and greatly reduces the loss.

distractorRationale.a: A solid core gives eddy currents the largest possible loops and the greatest heating
distractorRationale.c: Thin high-resistance wire increases copper (I²R) loss in the windings; it does not address eddy currents in the core
distractorRationale.d: D.c. would stop induction altogether, including the wanted secondary e.m.f.

questions.stem: For an ideal transformer,

options.text: $V_s I_s = 0$ because energy is stored in the core

questions.explanation: The induced voltages are in the ratio of the turns. Power in equals power out for the ideal case, $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$, which rearranges to $I_p / I_s = V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p$. The current ratio is the inverse of the voltage ratio: step up the voltage and you step down the current.

distractorRationale.a: This inverts the turns ratio relative to the voltages
distractorRationale.c: The current ratio is written the same way as the voltage ratio; it must be inverted because power is conserved
distractorRationale.d: An ideal transformer transfers energy; it does not store it as a net loss, so Vs Is equals Vp Ip, not zero

questions.stem: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary and 50 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 240 V. Assuming the transformer is ideal, calculate the secondary voltage. Give your answer in volts.
questions.explanation: $V_s = V_p \times N_s / N_p = 240 \times 50 / 500 = 24\ \text{V}$. Inverting the turns ratio would give 2400 V, which would be a step-up result even though Ns is smaller than Np.

questions.stem: Hysteresis loss in a transformer is reduced by making the core of
questions.explanation: Hysteresis loss is the energy used to reverse the domains in the core every a.c. cycle. Soft iron has a narrow hysteresis loop, so little energy is wasted per cycle, and it is easily magnetised and demagnetised. Hard steel has a wide loop (that is why it makes permanent magnets) and would run hot.

distractorRationale.a: Hard steel is used for permanent magnets precisely because it resists being demagnetised — the opposite of what a transformer core needs
distractorRationale.c: Copper is used for the windings (to cut I²R loss), not for the magnetic core; it is not ferromagnetic
distractorRationale.d: Wood is not ferromagnetic, so it cannot carry the flux from primary to secondary

questions.stem: Electrical power is transmitted over long distances at high voltage because

options.text: high voltage travels faster than low voltage
the current is then small, so $I^2 R$ heating in the cables is small
transformers work only at high voltage
the resistance of the cables falls when the voltage is raised

questions.explanation: Power $P = IV$, so for a fixed $P$ a high $V$ means a low $I$. Cable loss is $I^2 R$. Cutting the current by 10 cuts the heat loss by 100. That is why TCN lines run at 132 kV or 330 kV, with step-down transformers only near the consumers.

distractorRationale.a: Electromagnetic disturbances on the line travel at a speed set by the cable, not by the voltage
distractorRationale.c: Transformers work at any a.c. voltage; the 240 V pole transformer is a counter-example
distractorRationale.d: Cable resistance depends on material, length and thickness, not on the voltage applied

questions.stem: 100 kW of power is to be transmitted. Compared with transmission at 250 V, transmission at 25 kV reduces the current in the cables by a factor of
questions.explanation: $I = P/V$. At 250 V, $I = 100\,000 / 250 = 400\ \text{A}$. At 25 kV, $I = 100\,000 / 25\,000 = 4\ \text{A}$. The current falls by $400/4 = 100$, equal to the voltage ratio $25\,000/250 = 100$. The $I^2 R$ loss, however, falls by $100^2 = 10\,000$ — that is a different (and even more dramatic) factor, and it is the trap in option d.

distractorRationale.a: That would be the ratio of 2500 V to 250 V, not 25 kV to 250 V
distractorRationale.c: 250 is the low voltage in volts, not a ratio of the two currents
distractorRationale.d: 10 000 is the factor by which I²R loss falls, not the factor by which I itself falls

questions.stem: An ideal transformer has 1200 turns on the primary and 60 turns on the secondary. The primary current is 0.25 A. Calculate the secondary current. Give your answer in amperes.
questions.explanation: For an ideal transformer $I_s / I_p = N_p / N_s$, so $I_s = 0.25 \times 1200 / 60 = 0.25 \times 20 = 5.0\ \text{A}$. Using $N_s / N_p$ instead would give 0.0125 A, which is the wrong way round: this is a step-down of voltage and therefore a step-up of current.

questions.stem: The transformer equation relates the primary and secondary voltages to the number of turns in the primary and secondary coils. Which of the following equations correctly represents this relationship?
questions.explanation: The correct relationship is given by the equation V_p / V_s = N_p / N_s, where V_p and V_s are the primary and secondary voltages, and N_p and N_s are the number of turns in the primary and secondary coils, respectively. This equation is fundamental in understanding how transformers operate.

distractorRationale.b: This equation is incorrect as it reverses the relationship.
distractorRationale.c: This equation is incorrect because it implies a multiplication rather than a ratio.
distractorRationale.d: This equation is incorrect as it suggests addition rather than a ratio.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a method to reduce energy losses in a transformer?

options.text: Using a thicker wire for the windings
Increasing the frequency of the input voltage

questions.explanation: Using laminated cores is an effective method to reduce energy losses in a transformer, particularly hysteresis losses. Laminations reduce eddy currents, which in turn minimizes energy loss due to heat.

distractorRationale.b: Increasing frequency can lead to higher losses, not lower.
distractorRationale.c: High-resistance materials in the core would increase losses rather than reduce them.

distractorRationale.c: While safety is important, the primary reason for high voltage is to reduce losses.
distractorRationale.d: Transformer size is more related to the power level than the voltage used.
